studies.title: Made In Hardship
studies.meaning: Three oaths, and each is tied to the listener. The city he lives in, his own presence in it, and a parent with a child. Scholars differ over the second line, reading it as saying the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is a lawful resident of Mecca, or that the city's protections would be lifted against him. Then the claim the oaths support: the human being is made in hardship, a word covering both struggle and being made upright.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The city sworn by is Mecca, which had a recognised sanctuary where violence was not permitted, and the surah swears by it while the man addressed is living under threat inside it. The classical sources connect the second ayah to that tension without agreeing on its exact sense. The third oath, a parent and a child, is left unnamed, which the commentators discuss at length.

keyTerms.note: From a root for the liver and for the middle of a thing, and by extension for what is hard and dense. The word carries labour, and the classical readers also hear uprightness in it, a body built to stand.

From the root for untying and for what is released. The ambiguity is why scholars differ: it can mean a person who is settled and free in a place, or one for whom the place's protection has been lifted.
A negative particle attached to the verb of swearing. Grammarians read it as intensifying rather than negating, a formula for a solemn oath, and the same opening is used at the head of other surahs.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca was a sanctuary town where blood could not be shed and a hunted man could not be taken. That protection was the town's whole business model, since it made the fairs and the pilgrimage possible. Swearing by that city while its own protections were being bent around one resident put the oath and the situation in the same sentence, and everyone listening knew it.
studies.didYouKnow: The third oath names a parent and a child without naming either, and the classical commentators fill the gap in three ways: the first human and all who came after, Abraham and the son who helped him build the sanctuary, or simply every father and every child. The Quran leaves it open, and the range is preserved rather than resolved.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Hardship is described as the condition of creation rather than as a punishment or an accident. That single move changes what a difficult life means: it is not evidence of disfavour and does not require an explanation. The oaths that precede it are all local and small, a town, a man, a parent, so the largest claim in the passage is grounded in the most ordinary things the listener could see from where he stood.

crossReferences.why: Names what the hardship is for, an ascent the same surah describes a few lines later.
Makes the same claim about human life with a different word, effort that wears a person down.
Records the origin of the sanctuary sworn by here, a prayer for the same city's safety.

studies.applyIt: The next time you catch yourself thinking that life should be easier than this, try the sentence in this ayah as a working assumption for a day: it was made hard on purpose. Notice what stops being an emergency. The claim is not a comfort, but people generally find that expecting difficulty costs less energy than resenting it.

studies.title: Two Eyes And Two Lips
studies.meaning: A boast is quoted, not summarised. He says he has destroyed a heap of wealth, and the verb he picks is one of ruin rather than of giving, which the commentators read as the language of a man whose outlay is meant to sound heroic. The reply does not dispute the amount. It changes the subject to equipment he never bought: two eyes, a tongue, two lips, and a showing of the two high roads. Each item is ordinary, and every one of them was in place before there was any money to spend.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Standing in the city was built on visible outlay. A man who fed guests, slaughtered for a gathering, or paid a compensation another clan owed had that recited about him afterwards, and the amounts were part of the poem. Classical commentators read the quoted boast as the ordinary speech of that system rather than as one individual's vice, and no specific occasion is attached to the lines.

keyTerms.note: A verb of causing something to perish. He does not say he spent or gave; he says he annihilated it, which makes the outlay sound like a feat, and the Quran quotes the word rather than correcting it.
From a root of matting or pressing together until a mass holds its own shape. It pictures money as a pile rather than a sum, which is how a boaster naturally describes it.
A dual from a word for raised open ground where a track stays visible. It occurs only here in the Quran, and the commentators read it overwhelmingly of the two moral ways set before a person.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reputation in Mecca was audited in public. Camels slaughtered for guests, debts covered for a man with no clan behind him, a share taken in a caravan that failed: all of it was known, counted, and turned into verse. There was no privacy about generosity, which made generosity easy to fake and expensive to skip. The boast in this passage is the standard closing line of that whole performance.
studies.didYouKnow: The dual word for the two ways occurs only once in the Quran. It is a landscape term: high open ground where a path stays in sight, as opposed to a route through a ravine where you cannot see where you are going. The choice put before the person is therefore described as one made in full view rather than in the dark.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The answer to a boast about spending is an inventory of things received. That move reframes ownership itself, since the faculties listed are the instruments with which the wealth was earned and the boast was spoken. The last item shifts register: after four body parts comes a showing of two roads, so guidance is placed on the same list as eyes and lips, as standard issue rather than as a reward.

crossReferences.why: Lists hearing, sight and hearts as given to people who came out of the womb knowing nothing, so that they might be thankful.
Puts guidance to the way alongside the same freedom to be grateful or ungrateful about it.
Names the same faculties and closes with how little thanks is returned for them.

studies.applyIt: Close your eyes for thirty seconds in a room you know well and try to cross it. Then sit down and say nothing for a minute with your lips pressed shut. Both things you have had for free since before you can remember, and neither appears anywhere in the account you keep of what you have achieved.

studies.title: The Steep Pass
studies.meaning: A negative statement first: he did not storm the pass. The verb is violent, describing a rush at something steep, and it implies the ascent is taken at speed or not at all. Then the Quran interrupts itself to ask whether the reader knows what the ascent is, and the answer is a short list of concrete acts. None of them is a belief. The first is freeing a person, named by the word for a neck.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a surah that has just described a man boasting about how much wealth he consumed. Slavery was ordinary in Arabia, and freeing a person was a recognised act of piety that cost real money, since a slave was a capital asset. Hunger years were also recognised, and feeding during one meant giving away what your own household would need. No specific occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A verb for throwing yourself at something difficult without hesitating, used of a rider driving a horse into rough ground. It suggests the ascent is not managed carefully but rushed at.
A specific word for a mountain road climbing between rocks, the hard section of a journey. Naming it with the definite article makes it a known place, as though every listener has one.
The idiom uses the word for a neck to mean a person, and the verb means untying. Someone held is pictured as bound at the neck, so freeing them is described as an act done with the hands.
A rare noun for the condition of being hungry, occurring only here in the Quran. It names a day rather than a person, so what is specified is the moment when food is hardest to give away.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A mountain pass outside Mecca was a real thing, not a figure of speech. The routes north climbed between black rock, and a loaded camel took the steep sections slowly while the drivers walked. Everyone knew which passes were hard. Using that word for a moral act told the listener what kind of effort was meant: not sustained walking, but the short stretch where the ground goes up.
studies.didYouKnow: Five ayat in a row here end on the same rhyme, and the words chosen to carry it are unusual ones: the ascent, a neck, hunger, kinship, dust. The rhyme does part of the work, since the list arrives as a single sound repeated, and a listener hearing it once would have carried the whole sequence away.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The steep ascent is defined by actions rather than by states, and the actions chosen have a common feature: each transfers something a person owns to someone who cannot repay. Freedom, food, attention to a relative nobody else is helping. Belief is mentioned in the surah, but after this list rather than before it, which puts the ordering deliberately: the acts are named first and the faith is placed alongside them.

crossReferences.why: Completes the list this unit begins and adds belief and mutual counsel at the end of it.
Gives a longer version of the same list, including the freeing of necks among the acts named.
Shows the same act with the giver's motive attached, and the recipients overlap almost exactly.

studies.applyIt: Look at your own relatives before you look further afield. The ayah specifies an orphan of near kinship, which usually means the person in your family that everyone assumes someone else is handling. Work out who that is, and do one specific thing for them this month: a call, a bill, an afternoon.

studies.title: Counselling Patience And Mercy
studies.meaning: The list of hard acts ends with a person identified by dust, and then a connector meaning afterwards attaches something else to the list: being among those who believed. Commentators have long discussed that ordering, since the deeds are named first and the believing is joined by a particle implying sequence; the readings run from a plain chronology to a rhetorical ranking that puts belief highest by placing it last. What follows is not private. Two reciprocal verbs describe people holding each other to patience and to mercy.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Freeing a captive and feeding people in a hungry season were acts a wealthy Meccan could perform without altering anything he believed, and some did, as a matter of standing. The surah answers that directly by naming the acts first and then naming what turns them into an ascent. Classical sources give no occasion for these lines and read the closing pair of names as the chapter's summary.

keyTerms.note: Formed from the word for earth as a noun of place. It describes poverty as contact with the ground, nothing between the person and it, and the word occurs only here in the Quran.
A reciprocal form, so no one in the picture is only the giver of advice. The same verb closes another very short surah, where it carries truth and patience instead.
Built on the word for the right side, which in Arabic also carries blessing and good omen. Its counterpart in the next line is built from the word for the left, so the two names are one image.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Someone with no clan slept on open ground at the edge of the settlement, and the dust on him was the visible sign of it. Distribution of food ran through kin gatherings, so a man attached to nobody was not refused so much as never counted. The surah identifies him by the dust rather than by any status, which is exactly how he would have been picked out in the street.
studies.didYouKnow: The word translated here as destitution appears only once in the Quran, and grammatically it is a noun of place rather than a noun of condition. The language makes poverty somewhere a person is rather than something he has, which is why the translations reach for images of dust and ground instead of a number.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Belief and conduct are refused as separate categories, and the passage will not rank them cleanly either; the particle joining them has been argued over for centuries for precisely that reason. Then the two reciprocal verbs move everything outward. What is being described at the top of the ascent is not an admirable individual but a group of people who keep returning each other to patience and to mercy.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same reciprocal verb twice to close its argument, counselling one another to truth and to patience.
Refuses the same separation, defining righteousness by belief and by giving wealth away together.
Names the two companies by the same right and left imagery, expanded into a full description.

studies.applyIt: Ask one person this month to hold you to something small and specific, and offer to do the same for them. Not accountability in general: one thing, with a date. The verbs in this passage are reciprocal, which means the ascent it describes is not something the Quran expects anyone to climb by themselves.
